parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by a *magnetic field*.

markscheme_points.text: region where there is a force exerted on
a current-carrying conductor or a moving charge or a magnetic material/magnetic pole

hints: Hint 1: Think about how all fields are defined in physics - what test object do you place in the space to detect the field?
Hint 2: Remember a magnetic field does not exert a force on a stationary charge - what type of charge or object must be moving or magnetic to feel it?
parts.proper_answer: A region of space where a magnetic pole, a moving charge or a current-carrying conductor experiences a magnetic force.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a field means**
Think of a field as an invisible zone of influence. If you put a suitable test object in that zone, it feels a force without being touched. For gravity it is mass, for electric fields it is charge.

Step 2: **What feels a magnetic force**
For magnetism the test objects are different. A stationary charge feels nothing. You need a magnetised object like a magnetic pole, or a charge that is moving, which includes a current in a conductor. So you can say: $$ \text{magnetic field = region where } F \text{ acts on moving charge / current / pole} $$

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A rectangular piece of aluminium foil is situated in a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$, as shown in Fig. 9.1.

{{figure:figure_9_1}}

The magnetic field is normal to the face PQRS of the foil.

Electrons, each of charge $-q$, enter the foil at right angles to the face PQTV.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 9.1, shade the face of the foil on which electrons initially accumulate.
hints: Hint 1: Picture the electron velocity to the right and the $B$-field downwards, then apply Fleming's left-hand rule using conventional current in the opposite direction to electron motion.
parts.proper_answer: The face PSWV (the vertical side face containing P, S, W and V) is shaded.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort out directions**
Electrons move to the right into the foil. Magnetic flux density $B$ acts vertically downwards, normal to the large face PQRS. The magnetic force will push the electrons sideways, perpendicular to both.

Step 2: **Use Fleming's left-hand rule carefully**
Conventional current $I$ is opposite to electron motion, so $I$ points to the left. Point your First finger down for $B$, your seCond finger to the left for $I$. Your thuMb then points to the side face PSWV. That is the direction of the magnetic force $$F = Bqv$$ on the moving electrons, so electrons are initially driven to and accumulate on face PSWV.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Explain why electrons do not continuously accumulate on the face you have shaded.

markscheme_points.text: accumulating electrons cause an electric field (between the faces)
force due to electric field opposes force due to magnetic field
accumulation stops when magnetic force equals electric force

hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to the foil as a whole when many negative electrons pile up on one side - what does the other side become and what does this separation create across the foil?
Hint 2: Consider the new force that this separation exerts on the next electrons coming through - in which direction does it push them compared with the magnetic deflection?
Hint 3: Think about when the build-up must stop - what condition of the two opposing forces gives a steady Hall voltage with no further net sideways movement?
parts.proper_answer: Electrons accumulating on one face leave positive charge on the opposite face, setting up a transverse electric field. This field exerts an electric force on electrons opposite to the magnetic force. Accumulation stops when electric force equals magnetic force, so net transverse force is zero.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Charge separation builds an electric field**
At first the magnetic force $$F_B = Bqv$$ pushes every electron sideways to face PSWV. That face becomes negatively charged and the opposite face becomes positively charged. Separated charges always create an electric field $E$ across the foil, from positive to negative.

Step 2: **Electric force opposes magnetic force**
The new electric field pushes back on incoming electrons. The electric force $$F_E = qE$$ points away from the crowded negative face, i.e. opposite to the magnetic deflection force $F_B$.

Step 3: **Equilibrium stops further build-up**
As more electrons arrive, $E$ and $F_E$ grow. Very quickly $$qE = Bqv$$ and the net sideways force becomes zero. Electrons then pass straight through with no further accumulation. The steady potential difference left across the foil is the Hall voltage $V_H$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem:
The Hall voltage $V_{H}$ developed across the foil in (b) is given by the expression

$$V_{H} = \frac{BI}{ntq}$$

where $I$ is the current in the foil.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: State the meaning of the quantity $n$.
hints: Hint 1: Look at the units needed in $V_H = BI/ntq$ - what quantity counted per unit volume would involve the charge $q$ to give total mobile charge?
parts.proper_answer: Number of charge carriers (electrons) per unit volume.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Meaning of n**
In Hall theory and in $I = nAvq$, $n$ is always the concentration of mobile charges. It tells you how crowded the carriers are: $$n = \frac{\text{number of charge carriers}}{\text{volume}}$$ with unit $\text{m}^{-3}$. For aluminium it is very large because every atom contributes free electrons.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Using the letters on Fig. 9.1, identify the distance $t$.
hints: Hint 1: In the formula $t$ is the thickness of the slab measured along the direction of the $B$-field, which is normal to the large face PQRS - which short vertical edge on Fig. 9.1 fits that?
parts.proper_answer: PV (or QT or SW), the short vertical thickness of the foil parallel to B.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify t from geometry**
$B$ is normal to the large face PQRS, i.e. vertical in the diagram. In the derivation $t$ is the dimension of the conductor along $B$. That is the very thin vertical side of the foil. Using the labels this is $$t = PV = QT = SW$$

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Suggest why, in practice, Hall probes are usually made using a semiconductor material rather than a metal.

markscheme_points.text: (for semiconductor,) n is (much) smaller so VH (much) larger

hints: Hint 1: Look at where $n$ sits in $V_H = BI/ntq$ and compare typical carrier densities in metals and semiconductors to see what happens to $V_H$ for the same $B$ and $I$.
parts.proper_answer: In a semiconductor $n$ is much smaller than in a metal, so $V_H = BI/ntq$ is much larger and easier to measure.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why semiconductors give a bigger signal**
From $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq}$$ you can see $$V_H \propto \frac{1}{n}$$ A metal has a huge $n$, about $10^{28}$ $\text{m}^{-3}$, so $V_H$ is tiny, often microvolts. A semiconductor has far fewer mobile carriers, so for the same $B$ and $I$ the Hall voltage is much larger, millivolts or volts, and much more practical for a Hall probe.
